paras: The Ku Klux search of G. W. Witherspoon's house was a night raid in Jefferson County, Florida, around the November 1880 election, in which a masked and armed band entered and searched the home of Witherspoon, a Black Republican candidate for Congress, just after he had been forced to leave it. Witherspoon was driven from his county, and no one was reported hurt. The episode became known through a New York Times correspondent who offered it as an example of election fraud and violence in Florida's "Black Belt."

Writing from Jacksonville on November 15, the Times correspondent said that federal supervisors and marshals had been driven from polling places and that armed white men on horseback had charged on Black Republican voters. He named Madison, Jefferson, Leon, Gadsden and Jackson counties as the places where the frauds were most boldly carried out. In Jefferson County, according to his figures, the registration list showed a Republican majority of 2,300, yet the Republicans polled little more than 800 votes.

Witherspoon, described as "colored" and "running for congress," was "compelled to quit his bed at midnight and leave his county." He was hardly out of his house when a band of masked and armed men, whom the correspondent called "Ku-Klux," entered and searched it. At the same time the United States marshal in the county was forced to "take to the woods."

The correspondent wrote that names and facts were being withheld "pending prosecution" and predicted that the United States courts would be kept busy for a long time. He also expected Congress to seat Witherspoon from the second congressional district. No report of arrests, indictments or trials for the raid on Witherspoon's house appears in the coverage.

The only account is the Times letter, which Republican papers outside Florida reprinted: the Chicago Daily Tribune on November 22, the Knoxville Daily Chronicle on November 25 and the Ellsworth American in Maine on December 2. The Chicago and Knoxville papers headed it "The Farce in Florida" and "The Audacious Frauds in the Black Belt," while the Ellsworth American added a headline about "Bourbon Violence" and "Work for the Courts." The letter treated the raid as "only an instance" of Democratic lawlessness and argued that there was "no Solid South unless made so by shotguns and pistols in the hands of Democratic Ku-Klux."
No Florida paper's account of the raid was found, and the Black press of the period is not represented in the coverage.

reader.title: Ku Klux search of G. W. Witherspoon's house
bases: A masked, armed band searched the house of a Black congressional candidate at election time after he had been forced to leave his bed and his county; no injury or killing is reported (A2, A3, A4).
All three accounts are reprints of one Nov. 15 Jacksonville letter to the New York Times (A2, A3, A4); no independent or local Florida account was found.
